newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu and Kabila prepare to meet Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu and Kabila prepare to meet Saturday.

text.p: Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire and rebel leader Laurent Kabila prepared on Thursday for face-to-face talks at sea, with Kabila insisting the veteran strongman must stand down after three decades in power.
Zairean officials said the meeting, initially planned for Friday, would take place on Saturday. The venue remains a South African navy ship in international waters off Africa.
In New York, the U.N. Security Council welcomed the prospect of talks and urged rebels, who are marching on the capital Kinshasa, not to mistreat Rwandan Hutu refugees.

In signs of growing tension, the military governor of Kinshasa said anyone crossing the river to neighbouring Congo would need a special permit. Britain advised its nationals to leave while they still could.
Kabila left his headquarters in southeastern Zaire on Thursday to visit neighbouring countries in advance of the South African-brokered talks.
"The talks will just be about Mobutu and what we do with him. Our uncompromising demand is that he leaves power and we shall look after him," he told Reuters late on Wednesday.
There was no indication Mobutu was ready to step down.
Kabila spoke as his army advanced towards Kenge on the route to Kinshasa. He said Mobutu's army had begun blowing up bridges to try to slow the advance.
Aides said Mobutu, who is debilitated by cancer, had dropped plans to leave for Gabon on Thursday en route for the talks.
"This is not Zaire's decision and there's no health reason but we understand the talks have been postponed until Saturday," Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba told Reuters.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson told reporters in Kinshasa on Wednesday there were no preconditions for the talks, to be chaired by President Nelson Mandela of South Africa.

At rebel headquarters in Lubumbashi, officials said Kabila was surprised Richardson had said "several African leaders" would attend the talks on the supply ship SAS Outeniqua. The rebels do not want the talks to turn into a mini-summit.

The Mobutu camp views Richardson's mediation with some cynicism since it believes the United States plotted with African countries, led by Uganda and Rwanda, to end his rule. Mobutu, 66, seized power in 1965 with backing from Washington, which saw him as a Third World bulwark against Communism.

Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, did not persuade Kabila to accept a truce ahead of talks or a transitional government before elections -- key components of a U.N. peace plan devised by its special envoy, Mohamed Sahnoun, who will attend the talks.

Kabila's rebels took up arms last October and now control over half of Zaire. They have made short shrift of Mobutu's ragged army and stand poised to attack Kinshasa from their new forward base at Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) to the east.
They grabbed Bumba, south of Gbadolite, with no resistance on Tuesday and were set to take Mobutu's nearby birth-place at Lisala, residents in radio contact with Kinshasa said.

The war has trapped Hutu refugees, who fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide of Tutsis. Critics accuse Zaire's Tutsi-dominated rebels of killing refugees -- or at least leaving them to die.

The Security Council urged rebel cooperation with U.N. investigations and welcomed a Kabila commitment to act against rebels "who violate the rules of international humanitarian law concerning the treatment of refugees and civilians."
Zairean rebels handed over 62 Rwandan refugee children and adults after a U.N. demand to know the fate of some 110 people abducted from a paediatric hospital near Bukavu, a UNICEF spokesman said.
